claims.text: Enhanced atomic-scale configurational disorder introduces local lattice distortions in single-phase superconducting high-entropy alloys.
Disorder-induced local lattice distortions increase electron–phonon coupling.
Stronger electron–phonon coupling raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Rapid solidification maximizes configurational randomness relative to controlled annealing.
Controlled annealing induces short-range atomic order while preserving overall composition.
Random site occupancy produces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions alter the phonon density of states.
Local lattice distortions alter scattering mechanisms.
Changes in the phonon density of states and scattering enhance electron–phonon interactions.
Increased configurational disorder creates local lattice-strain variations that modify the phonon spectrum.
The modified phonon spectrum produces a stronger electron–phonon coupling constant.
Electron–phonon coupling is responsible for Cooper-pair formation in the proposed alloy regime.
Rapidly solidified, maximally disordered samples will have a higher Tc than compositionally identical samples annealed to promote short-range order.
Maximally disordered samples will exhibit stronger superconducting-gap features than the annealed baseline.
The proposed relationship applies only while disorder remains below the threshold for Anderson localization.
The proposed relationship requires retention of a homogeneous single-phase structure.
The proposed relationship requires electron–phonon coupling to be the dominant superconducting pairing mechanism.
Phase separation, composition changes, or excessive disorder may introduce mechanisms outside the hypothesis.
Disorder may counteract superconductivity through pair breaking or localization.
Failure of increased disorder to produce both stronger electron–phonon coupling and higher Tc relative to the annealed control would falsify the hypothesis.
